implementation_notes: mockall generates a mock type from a trait (#[automock]) or from mock! for what it cannot handle; the test sets expectations before the call - mock.expect_foo().with(predicate::eq(4)).times(1).returning(|x| x + 1) - and any access contrary to them panics. What replaces the classic spy object is the generated expectation struct: the argument record is expressed as predicate matchers rather than inspected after the fact, and a hand-rolled recorder is the alternative when post-hoc assertions matter more than the DSL.
pitfalls: Expectations must be declared before the call; an unexpected call panics immediately, so failures surface at the call site rather than at an assertion.
Traits with generic methods or non-'static references cannot be automocked; fall back to mock! with explicit types or to a recording struct.
Expectation methods take &mut self, so a mock shared across threads needs a Mutex and concurrent-call tests must serialise their setup.

variants.name: Hand-rolled recording impl behind Box<dyn Trait>
variants.idiom_name: struct + RefCell<Vec<Call>> implementing the trait, asserted after
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of (or alongside) mockall, the Rust spy is an ordinary struct implementing the collaborator trait: it holds a RefCell<Vec<Call>> (or a Mutex when shared), forwards to the real implementation when it owns one, and the test asserts on the recorded calls after the SUT ran - the action-then-assertion shape mockall's expectation DSL does not offer. Rust's ownership model makes forwarding explicit: the recorder owns or borrows the production object, and Box<dyn Trait> is the usual collaborator type at the seam.
pitfalls: RefCell borrowing panics if the SUT re-enters the recorder while the test iterates the log - scope the borrow or switch to Mutex.
Nothing checks that the recorder still matches the trait after the trait grows; keep a contract test or delegate to a real instance to catch drift.
